views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold current tariff posture but do not escalate further. Engage seriously in the October talks with Liu He. The scheduled mid-September preparatory discussions and early-October ministerial round represent the best near-term window to extract concessions without further self-harm. Resist pressure to raise existing List 3 rates to 30% on October 1 — use that threatened hike as leverage, not as a committed action.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.3 reflects a real but not yet existential situation. On the negative side, US manufacturing is in a technical recession (two consecutive quarters of contraction per Fed data; ISM manufacturing index at its lowest since Jan 2016 in August). UBS economist Seth Carpenter warns the trade war has brought the US 'to the brink of recession,' with imports of targeted goods down 40% and consumer spending consistently weak since tariffs began. Farm aid has reached $28B, soybean exports to China are at their lowest since 2002, and List 4A (Sept 1) now directly taxes consumer goods — raising costs for households. The tariff cost is borne almost entirely by US importers and consumers, not by China (per Amiti, Redding, Weinstein research showing full pass-through). On the other hand, the US economy is not in broad recession — services remain strong, unemployment is historically low at ~3.7%, and manufacturing is only ~11% of GDP. The US retains significant leverage: China's economy is slowing more sharply, and Beijing has shown willingness to make small goodwill gestures (Sept 11-13 tariff exemptions on industrial inputs and farm goods) ahead of the October round.

The action score of -0.1 (borderline hold/negotiate) reflects the strategic calculus that escalation from here carries more downside risk than upside. Raising List 3 to 30% on October 1 would hit US businesses and consumers harder than it pressures Beijing, especially given Xi Jinping's signals of preparing for 'protracted struggle.' But full concession is premature — the US still has leverage, China is engaging, and the October talks have not yet begun. The right posture is firm engagement: maintain current tariff levels as leverage, negotiate seriously, and condition any rollback on concrete Chinese commitments on structural IP/tech-transfer issues and enforcement mechanisms — the sticking points that collapsed talks in May.
